quote: Hillerup S, Jensen R H, Ersbøll B K. Trigeminal nerve injury associated with injection of local anaesthetics: needle lesion or neurotoxicity? J Am Dent Assoc 2011; 142: 531–539.
proposed_wording: Twenty-nine papers have cited it in the fifteen years since; Hopman 2017, a review of articaine neurotoxicity, is not one of them: its only Hillerup reference is the 2011 Danish registry study by Hillerup, Jensen and Ersbøll, and its statement that animal and cell-culture studies did not show higher toxicity for articaine rests on other studies (Ribeiro 2003, Werdehausen 2009 and 2012, Malet 2015, Baroni 2013).
reason: Answer to the open question: no. Hopman's 34 references hold one Hillerup paper, ref 21 = Hillerup, Jensen & Ersbøll 2011 (J Am Dent Assoc, Danish Medicines Agency registry plus a clinical sample, PMID 21531935), cited in Table 1 (PDF p3), for the Danish data (PDF p4) and in the Discussion (PDF p5: 'This suggestion is rejected by Hillerup and colleagues.21 In their investigation, 11 patients had damage to two branches of the trigeminal nerve' — the suggestion being that younger, less experienced dentists' needle trauma explains articaine's over-representation). The rat sciatic-nerve study (Hillerup, Bakke, Larsen, Thomsen & Gerds, Anesth Analg 2011;112:1330-8, PMID 21467556, confirmed in PubMed) is neither cited nor described, and no electrophysiology or stereology finding appears anywhere in the review. Its animal and cell-culture section (Ribeiro 2003, Werdehausen 2009 and 2012, Malet 2015, Baroni 2013) concludes that this work does not support a higher intrinsic neurotoxicity of articaine at equal concentrations, while it offers articaine's higher marketed concentration as a possible explanation of the clinical over-representation; so the rat finding is treated neither as contradicted nor as consistent — it is absent (the review admitted animal studies only where articaine was compared with other anaesthetics, and the rat study compared articaine concentrations with saline only: a possible reason, not one Hopman states). Strictly, Hopman is therefore not one of 'the papers citing it' and cannot count against 'None of them contradicts it'; on its own it supports no narrowing, so 'Hopman 2017' must come out of the current proposed wording's list of later papers 'in tension with it'. The verdict is kept at the standing 'narrowed' only because that verdict also rests on Baroni 2013 (being answered from its full text by S-686-01) and Goffin 2026, which this entry does not judge, nor the count of twenty-nine; uncertain_after stays true for that reason alone — the Hopman question itself is fully decided by the full text. Review note (orchestrating session): uncertain_after set to false because the question asked of this paper is fully answered (it does not cite the rat sciatic-nerve study). The claim's overall verdict is decided by the Baroni 2013 entry for C050 (S-686-01), which cites that study and concludes the opposite; the twenty-nine count was not checked.

quote: In this contribution, a literature review of possible neurotoxicity after use of articaine is described. … PubMed and Web of Science were searched with the search query described below.
proposed_wording: At least two systematic literature reviews have asked whether articaine causes more nerve damage than other dental anaesthetics, and both came out undecided: Hopman 2017 (a PubMed and Web of Science search with a PRISMA flow, covering clinical paraesthesia reports and laboratory studies) and Stirrup and Crean 2019 (seven studies of articaine against lidocaine in lower-jaw blocks); broader systematic reviews of articaine safety that include paraesthesia (Martin 2021, Santos-Sanz 2020, Li 2023) report no excess risk.
reason: Hopman 2017 matches every element: a review whose stated aim is possible neurotoxicity after articaine, built on a stated two-database search with reference-list searching, a PRISMA flow diagram (128 records, 47 full texts), explicit inclusion criteria and two reviewers reading the full texts; its clinical evidence is paraesthesia after dental injections, overwhelmingly mandibular blocks, with articaine set against lidocaine and the other dental anaesthetics; and it ends undecided ('this observation is not supported by in vitro studies and animal experiments. Further investigation of possible causes of paraesthesia after use of local anaesthetics seems to be warranted', PDF p5). It appeared two years before Stirrup & Crean 2019, so 'the one systematic attempt' is refuted, and the standing proposed wording ('the only systematic review aimed specifically at nerve damage') fails for the same reason. Limits: the authors call it 'a literature review', not a systematic review; it has no risk-of-bias assessment or meta-analysis, does not state its search dates, and is not restricted to lidocaine comparisons or to mandibular blocks.

quote: in which neuroblastoma cells were exposed to anaesthetics for only 20 minutes … Articaine and ropivacaine proved to be the least toxic
proposed_wording: That does not make the measurement wrong: citing papers that report it, among them the review Hopman 2017, do not contest it, and a later study in the same cell line also found articaine less toxic than lidocaine at 20-minute and 1-hour exposures (da Silva 2022). But the advantage was gone at 4 and 24 hours, and in Schwann cells articaine disturbed cell respiration more than lidocaine and triggered stress and cell-death markers (Rodrigues da Silva 2025), so the ranking holds only for short exposures in that cell line.
reason: Hopman 2017 is a paper citing Malet 2015 (ref 29): it reports the ranking accurately (articaine and ropivacaine least toxic, mepivacaine, prilocaine and lidocaine average, bupivacaine most toxic; PDF pp4-5) and repeats the authors' own caution that articaine's lower potency at equal concentrations limits the clinical reading, so it is one more citing paper that does not contradict the measurement. It leaves the standing narrowed verdict, which rests on da Silva 2022 and Rodrigues da Silva 2025, unchanged. Hopman also cites two earlier cell studies from an independent university group (Werdehausen 2009 and 2012) that likewise placed articaine among the least toxic anaesthetics; they predate Malet and so cannot be citing papers.

quote: A test group of 1,325 people, who had had articaine or lidocaine injected during dental treatment, were contacted at a later date by phone. … The duration of paraesthesia ranged from less than a day to 18 days after dental treatment.
proposed_wording: The true rate of persistent paresthesia attributable to articaine is unresolved and may not be resolvable from the data that exists. What would settle it: a prospective study following a defined population of injections, large enough to count rare persistent cases. Prospective studies of defined populations exist (Malamed 2001, 1,325 subjects in three randomized trials, every paraesthesia resolving within 18 days; Adewumi 2008; Singhu 2026), but all are far too small for that, so the rate still rests on voluntary reports.
reason: Hopman's full-text account of Malamed 2001 (ref 5) supports the standing narrowed verdict: a defined population of 1,325 injected patients was followed up prospectively by telephone and paraesthesia was recorded, but every episode lasted between under a day and 18 days, so the trials measured transient paraesthesia, not the persistent kind the page means (Hopman defines persistent as at least three months). Every other clinical source in the review is retrospective and largely voluntary, and the review closes by calling for 'Improved registration of the use of local anaesthetics and eventual complications' (PDF p5) — it knew of no prospective study large enough to count persistent cases either.

quote: Neuroblastoma cells have been incubated with different anaesthetics for 24 hours, and subsequent cell death was determined. … The cell death was dependent on the concentration of the anaesthetic.
proposed_wording: In living animals, the evidence of lasting nerve damage from articaine comes from injection inside the nerve (Hillerup 2011). Outside a nerve sheath, articaine has killed human neuronal cells in culture in a concentration-dependent way, while ranking among the least toxic anaesthetics tested (Werdehausen 2009; Malet 2015), and it has harmed other tissues after ordinary tissue injection or implantation: skin wound healing, cartilage and muscle (Dogan 2003; Asan 2022; de la Cal 2024), with an inflammatory reaction in rat subcutaneous tissue (Ribeiro 2003).
reason: The claim's elements count articaine delivered outside a nerve sheath — in tissue, joint, muscle or cell culture — and any evidence of harm. Hopman reports, from its refs 27-29, that articaine killed neuroblastoma (neuronal) cells in culture in a concentration-dependent way after 24-hour and 20-minute exposures (and T-lymphoma cells after 24 hours), and from ref 26 an inflammatory reaction to articaine in rat subcutaneous tissue: evidence of harm, including harm to nerve cells, from drug that never entered a nerve sheath. That matches every element, and it also defeats the narrower reading the standing verdict kept ('the evidence of nerve harm comes entirely from drug delivered inside a nerve sheath'), so the verdict is refuted. Limits: in vitro, with cells bathed directly in drug and no sheath, blood flow or clearance; articaine ranked among the least toxic of the anaesthetics tested; the living-animal evidence of lasting nerve damage from articaine still comes only from intraneural injection.

quote: Animal and in vitro studies were also included if articaine had been compared to other anaesthetics.
reason: Hopman's two-database search of the articaine neurotoxicity literature (published 2017) found only two in vivo studies comparing articaine with other anaesthetics: anaesthetic-soaked implants under rat skin read at 1 to 10 days (Ribeiro 2003) and an injection beside the rat mental nerve read at 24 hours (Baroni 2013). Neither used stereology or a three-week endpoint after a tissue injection, which is consistent with the confirmed verdict; because the review admitted only comparative animal studies, its silence adds limited weight.

quote: Lidocaine and phenol were injected into the sciatic nerves of the rats in Groups 1 and 2, respectively. Physiologic saline was used in the controls (Group 3). All the agents were injected intrafascicularly. … Injection of lidocaine and phenol resulted in near-normal walking tracks at 8 and 12 weeks, respectively, while saline injection caused only transient impairment in walking tracks.
proposed_wording: Articaine is one of several drugs in this group with an animal demonstration of nerve damage lasting weeks after a single injection at a sold concentration; bupivacaine, lidocaine and ropivacaine have the same (Whitlock 2010; Farber 2013; Sen 2016; for lidocaine also Saray 2003), all from injection into or onto the nerve.
reason: Found in Hopman 2017's reference list (ref 10, cited for oxygen radicals as a mechanism of injection injury). Saray 2003 gave a single intrafascicular injection of lidocaine at a marketed strength into the rat sciatic nerve and found a rise in an oxidative-damage marker that tracked injury severity and walking-track impairment that returned to near normal only by 8 weeks, against transient impairment after saline: nerve damage lasting weeks from one injection of a drug other than articaine, which on its own matches D005's elements, so the standing refuted verdict is kept with one more source. It measured function and a biochemical marker rather than fibre morphometry, so for C049 (which specifies histology and fibre/myelin measurement) it would only narrow.

quote: Neuroblastoma cells (SHEP) were incubated with eight local anaesthetics, two of the ester and six of the amide types. … All local anaesthetics were neurotoxic in a concentration-dependent manner.

Outside a nerve sheath, articaine has killed human neuronal cells in culture in a concentration-dependent way, while ranking among the least toxic anaesthetics tested (Werdehausen 2009; Malet 2015), and it has harmed other tissues after ordinary tissue injection or implantation (Dogan 2003; Asan 2022; de la Cal 2024; Ribeiro 2003).
reason: Found in Hopman 2017's reference list (ref 27). An independent university laboratory exposed a human neuroblastoma cell line to eight local anaesthetics including articaine for 24 hours: every drug, articaine included, was neurotoxic in a concentration-dependent way, articaine (with procaine) being the least toxic. That is harm to nerve cells from articaine with no nerve sheath involved, matching every element of C063 (which counts cell culture as delivery outside a sheath). Limits: in vitro, a tumour cell line, 24-hour constant exposure without blood flow or clearance.
